paras: The threatened lynching of J. M. Garrison took place at Winfield, Du Page County, Illinois, in late November 1881, when farmers who supplied his cheese factory gathered with a rope to hang him after the factory burned. Garrison's creditors accused him of setting the fire to avoid paying them, but the county sheriff intervened and took him to jail at Wheaton. Chicago dispatches about his escape were reprinted under headings such as "Escaped Lynching" in papers from Delaware to Minnesota and Wisconsin.

Garrison ran the Winfield cheese factory and collected money on behalf of the farmers who were its patrons, holding it over between payments. By his own account the October collections were behind, and the dividends owed to the Winfield farmers ran from $20 to $500 per claim and several thousand dollars in all. Other reports put the total owed at $10,000 or at about $1,000.

According to an Elgin dispatch to the Chicago Tribune, the factory burned "in a mysterious manner" on Wednesday night, November 23. Garrison told the Tribune that he had hidden $7,000 in greenbacks on the second floor to pay his patrons the next day, and that his helper Frank Burroughs woke about midnight to find the boiler room in flames and the money beyond reach. Earlier reports quoted him as saying $4,000 had burned.

The next day some patrons had Garrison arrested for arson, and before he could be taken to Wheaton a large number of farmers gathered in an angry mood. Someone suggested hanging him, a rope was procured, and the crowd started for the station where he was held. Most reports credited the sheriff of Du Page County, with a posse in one wire version, for stopping the crowd and hurrying Garrison to jail. Garrison himself said that "a little 'sand' and a revolver in my pocket" had saved him, while the Tribune added that the arrival of Judge Drummond, who lived near Winfield, probably helped calm the farmers.

Garrison and his cheesemaker were held in jail at Wheaton, though a Chicago correspondent wrote that his father was jailed with him. Brought before the justice of the peace at Wheaton, Garrison obtained a continuance. No report of the hearing's outcome appears in the coverage.

The Chicago Tribune broke the story in a short dispatch headed "An Alleged Incendiary" and followed it the next day with "Garrison's Grit," which gave Garrison's explanation at length. That follow-up presented the farmers as men "who had waited so patiently for their money" and became "enraged beyond control," without condemning the threat. Condensed wire versions ran as "Saved From Being Lynched" in the Wilmington Daily Gazette and as "Escaped Lynching" in the Mower County Transcript, the Watertown Republican and the Superior Times, while the St. Paul Daily Globe carried a one-paragraph brief.

The Memphis Public Ledger's Chicago correspondent treated the affair lightly, writing that a "lynching matinee came very near being one of the amusements down at Winfield." None of the reports mentioned Garrison's race or that of the crowd.

The reports differ on the loss, which the Tribune gave as $6,000 uninsured and the wire version as $5,000 with full insurance. They also differ on the night of the fire, Wednesday in the Tribune and Garrison's account but "the night of the 24th" in the wire version, and the local Tribune dispatch is the more direct source.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of J. M. Garrison
bases: A crowd of creditors procured a rope and threatened to hang Garrison, accused of burning his factory, until officers intervened (A1, A2, A4); no killing occurred.
Garrison was not killed: the crowd that threatened to hang him for alleged arson was stopped by the sheriff or by officers (A1, A4, A7), so this was a threatened lynching only (A2).

An Elgin special dispatch (A1), a separate Chicago wire (A4), Garrison's interview (A2) and a Chicago correspondent's letter (A7) agree that creditors threatened to lynch him with a rope after the fire.

accounts.label: Elgin special dispatch / wire
accounts.gist: Creditors openly charged Garrison with firing the factory, threatened to lynch him with a rope ready, and were stopped by the sheriff, who jailed him at Wheaton.

accounts.label: Garrison's account
accounts.gist: He held $7,000 to pay patrons, which burned in a midnight fire; a crowd got a rope after his arrest, and he credited 'a little sand' and a revolver with saving him, though the Tribune added that Judge Drummond's arrival pacified the farmers.

accounts.label: Chicago correspondent
accounts.gist: Creditors owed about $1,000 accused him of incendiary fraud, and it took 'several of officers of the law' to save his life.

framing.detail: The Tribune's first dispatch, headed 'An Alleged Incendiary', reported the creditors' charge and the threat without comment.
'Garrison's Grit' gave Garrison's explanation at length and treated the farmers' anger as understandable ('waited so patiently for their money').
Short wire briefs headed 'Saved From Being Lynched' and 'Escaped Lynching' ran in Delaware, Minnesota and Wisconsin papers.
The Memphis Public Ledger's Chicago correspondent wrote facetiously of a 'lynching matinee' as one of Winfield's 'amusements'.
